taxonomy.subtopic: Efferent arteriolar dependence on angiotensin II in bilateral renal artery stenosis

questions.stem_html: A 74-year-old man with diffuse atherosclerotic disease has resistant hypertension and bilateral abdominal bruits. Two days after an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is added, his serum creatinine concentration rises from 1.3 to 2.4 mg/dL. The accompanying diagram compares glomerular arteriolar tone before and after treatment. Which change most directly explains the fall in glomerular filtration rate?

options.text_html: Dilation of the efferent arteriole lowers glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
Constriction of the afferent arteriole increases filtration fraction
Dilation of the afferent arteriole lowers renal plasma flow
Constriction of the efferent arteriole decreases glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure
Increased mesangial-cell contraction expands the filtration surface area

questions.explanation_html: When renal perfusion pressure is reduced by bilateral renal artery stenosis, angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent arteriole and helps preserve glomerular capillary pressure. Blocking angiotensin II formation dilates the efferent arteriole, causing a marked decline in intraglomerular pressure and glomerular filtration rate.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Afferent constriction would reduce renal plasma flow and glomerular pressure, but it is not the characteristic immediate effect of ACE inhibition.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Afferent dilation tends to increase renal plasma flow and glomerular pressure.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Efferent constriction raises, rather than lowers, glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure over the physiologic range.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Mesangial contraction decreases the filtration surface area; ACE inhibition does not acutely cause this mechanism.

questions.educational_objective: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, glomerular filtration becomes dependent on angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction; ACE inhibition can therefore sharply reduce GFR.

media.alt_text: Side-by-side glomerular diagrams showing angiotensin II-supported efferent constriction before ACE inhibition and efferent dilation with reduced glomerular pressure afterward.
